transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
I can’t slow down—I have too many important things to take care of and I feel driven to keep doing more, day and night. Everyone is counting on me, and I just can't afford to stop.

Have you ever had a similar episode before, or have you ever had times when your mood was very high or irritable for several days and it caused problems? Also, during this time have you had any hallucinations or beliefs that others said were not true?

These experiences only happen when I get revved up like this, never when I'm my normal, calmer self. Lately, I just know in my gut that if I'm not personally watching every chart and pill, the doctors will make mistakes and my patients and parents will die, even though everyone tells me everything is fine. And I keep hearing a man's voice right behind my ear whispering, "Don't sleep, they're counting on you," when there's absolutely no one there!
Have you ever had a similar episode like this before, with high energy or irritability, lasting several days or longer, even if you did not have hallucinations or delusions?
No, I have never had an episode like this before in my life. In the past, I've always felt like my normal, calmer self. This intense state of high energy and irritability is completely new to me.
How long has this high-energy, irritable state been going on continuously, and has it lasted at least one week?

It has been going on continuously for about two months now, ever since I started taking all those extra shifts and managing my parents' appointments. So yes, it has lasted much longer than a week and hasn't let up at all.

latest_inference.note: Previously the only candidate was F30.2, and the new information supports keeping it unchanged. The episode is clearly elevated/irritable with increased activity lasting about two months, with grandiose responsibility, decreased need for sleep, and psychotic features (both delusional beliefs and auditory hallucinations) occurring only during the mood episode. There is no history of prior similar episodes, and there is no evidence provided of a primary psychotic disorder or another cause, so the current candidate remains F30.2.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a new-onset, sustained manic syndrome lasting about 2 months with markedly increased energy/drive, decreased need to stop/rest implied by nonstop activity, and clear mood-congruent psychotic symptoms including persecutory/grandiose delusional beliefs and auditory hallucinations. This is most consistent with manic episode with psychotic symptoms (severe mania).
